prose_changes.old: At a small monastery in the forest near Kozelsk, south of Moscow, a hermitage founded in 1821 became the center of something Russian Orthodoxy had never had at this scale. Elders — startsy — who kept the door open to anyone who walked up to it. Peasants, students, landowners and novelists queued outside the cell of Father Ambrose, and the elders who could not see everyone answered by letter, leaving thousands of pages of spiritual direction addressed not to monks but to ordinary people trying to live ordinary lives. They were also publishers: from the 1840s, with the Slavophile thinker Ivan Kireevsky, Optina ran a press that put the Greek ascetic fathers into Russian and made a monastic literature available to laypeople for the first time. Dostoevsky came in 1878 after the death of his small son, and turned what he found there into the elder Zosima.
prose_changes.new: At a small monastery in the forest near Kozelsk, south of Moscow, a hermitage was founded in 1821. It became the center of something Russian Orthodoxy had never had at this scale. Elders, called startsy, kept the door open to anyone who walked up to it. Peasants, students, landowners and novelists queued outside the cell of Father Ambrose. The elders could not see everyone, so they answered by letter. They left thousands of pages of spiritual advice. They wrote not to monks but to ordinary people trying to live ordinary lives. prose_changes.old: Under Ottoman rule the Orthodox of the Balkans had been governed as a single religious community answering to the Patriarch of Constantinople. The Greek revolt of 1821 — which opened with the hanging of Patriarch Gregory V at the gate of his own residence — broke that arrangement apart, and as each new nation won independence its church claimed self-government. Greece declared its church self-governing in 1833 and was formally recognized by Constantinople in 1850, Bulgaria won an imperial decree creating a national exarchate in 1870, Serbia was recognized in 1879 and Romania in 1885. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned phyletism — organizing the church by ethnic nation rather than by place — even as national churches went on multiplying anyway. What the century produced was not one church breaking up so much as a family of them, each with its own synod, its own language of worship, and its own claim on a people.
prose_changes.new: Under Ottoman rule, the Orthodox of the Balkans were governed as one religious community. That community answered to the Patriarch of Constantinople. The Greek revolt of 1821 broke this order apart. Weeks after the rising began, Patriarch Gregory V was hanged at the gate of his own home. As each new nation won its freedom, its church claimed the right to govern itself. Greece declared its church free in 1833, and Constantinople formally accepted it in 1850. Bulgaria won a decree from the sultan in 1870 that set up a national church, the exarchate. Serbia won its own church in 1879 and Romania in 1885. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned phyletism, which means building the church around a nation rather than a place. Even so, national churches kept on spreading. The century did not simply break one church apart. It made a family of churches. Each had its own synod, its own language of worship and its own claim on a people.
